title: The OECD Just Said What Everyone Feared. A Long War Could Trigger the Worst Slowdown Since the Pandemic.
excerpt: If the Middle East conflict drags into 2027, global growth could fall to 2.1 percent — with Asia, and India in particular, bearing the heaviest burden.
body:
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development issued its starkest warning yet on Wednesday: if the war in the Middle East drags into 2027, global growth will fall to levels rarely seen outside of catastrophic crises. Parts of Asia — including India — would be among the hardest hit.

In its June quarterly outlook, the OECD projected global growth of 2.8 percent for 2026 in its baseline scenario, which assumes Gulf oil and gas production begins recovering in the third quarter and the Strait of Hormuz gradually reopens. Even that optimistic reading represents a sharp slowdown from the 3.4 percent expansion recorded in 2025.

But the darker scenario is the one keeping policymakers awake. If energy disruptions persist well into next year, growth could collapse to 2.1 percent in 2026 and 1.8 percent in 2027. That would be the weakest performance this century outside of the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic.

## The India Problem

The OECD singled out Asian countries reliant on Middle Eastern energy supplies as the most vulnerable. India, which sourced more than 40 percent of its crude through the Strait of Hormuz before the conflict, falls squarely into that category.

The impact runs deeper than fuel prices. Higher energy costs are feeding into fertiliser prices, pushing up food costs in a country where food and energy constitute a larger share of household spending than in developed economies. The OECD noted that developing nations face a disproportionate burden precisely because "higher shares of energy and food in household consumption" leave less room for absorption.

India's GDP grew 7.2 percent in the January-March quarter — the fastest rate among major economies. But that number reflects a period before the full impact of the Hormuz disruption was felt. The RBI faces its most difficult rate decision in years, caught between rising oil-driven inflation, a weakening rupee, and a monsoon season that is already running late.

## Inflation, Rates and the AI Boom at Risk

If the conflict persists, global inflation could rise by 0.4 percentage points in 2026 and 1.3 percentage points in 2027, the OECD said. Central banks would likely respond with rate hikes of 0.5 to 0.75 percentage points — reversing the easing cycle that many had anticipated.

In its baseline scenario, the OECD expects G20 inflation to peak at 4 percent this year before easing to 3.1 percent in 2027. Interest rates would remain largely on hold this year, with cuts expected next year. In the protracted scenario, those cuts would not come.

The report also flagged an unexpected casualty of prolonged conflict: the global AI investment boom. Energy prices make up roughly 60 percent of data centre operating costs, and semiconductor manufacturing is both energy-intensive and dependent on Gulf-sourced by-products like helium and aluminium. The OECD warned of a potential "market repricing" of AI supply chain companies — firms like SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung, which have become trillion-dollar companies on the back of AI demand.

"The longer the disruptions last, the larger the economic and social costs become," OECD chief economist Stefano Scarpetta said. "Duration matters a lot for the economic and social consequences."

## The Ceasefire That Isn't

The timing of the OECD's warning is pointed. Just last week, the United States and Iran announced a tentative initial agreement to halt hostilities. But the two sides have not signed anything. Iranian media reported that Tehran has not communicated with Washington for several days. Trump insists negotiations continue.

On Wednesday, the ceasefire was tested again. Iranian missiles struck Kuwait's airport, killing one person and injuring more than 60. Bahrain intercepted three missiles and several drones. The U.S. military carried out strikes near the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude climbed above $98, inching toward $100 a barrel.

The OECD's message is less a forecast than a price tag. Every week the Strait of Hormuz remains closed costs the global economy billions. Every month without a durable ceasefire makes the protracted scenario more likely. For India, the calculation is simpler still: a country that imports 85 percent of its oil cannot afford a war it did not start to become permanent.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For Indians abroad, the OECD report is a signal to watch three things closely: the rupee, the RBI's upcoming rate decision, and oil prices. If Brent crosses $100 sustainably, the cascading effects on Indian equities, real estate, and remittance purchasing power will be significant. Indian IT companies with high energy costs in their data centre operations face margin pressure. And the AI investment narrative that has powered stock markets to record highs in Tokyo, Taipei, and New York may face its first serious test.
author: Diaspora Desk
